voice.text: In The Jungle Book, Rikki-tikki the little mongoose fights the great cobra — and <emphasis>wins</emphasis>. [pause] How can a small furry animal beat a giant snake? Tap your guess.

Rikki-tikki wins with <emphasis>physical adaptations</emphasis> — body parts he was born with. [pause] Lightning speed to dodge the strike. Thick, coarse fur that is hard to bite through. A tough body that even the cobra can barely hurt.
The tiger has one too: stripes. In tall grass they melt away — that is <emphasis>camouflage</emphasis>, a body pattern it was born with. Physical.

Now something different. One wolf cannot catch a big deer — but the pack hunts <emphasis>together</emphasis>. Hunting together is a thing wolves <emphasis>do</emphasis>, not a body part. That is a <emphasis>behavioral</emphasis> adaptation. [pause] The bear's long winter sleep is behavioral too.

Can a whole population change? Yes — but slowly. [pause] One year, only big hard seeds are left. Birds with bigger beaks can crack them; they survive, and have chicks. Many, many generations later, most of the birds have big beaks. [pause] No bird <emphasis>chose</emphasis> to change. It happened over a long, long time.

How do we know about animals from long, long ago? <emphasis>Fossils</emphasis> — living things turned to stone are clues. [pause] A fish fossil high on a mountain tells a story: this land was once under water.
An adaptation appears. Is it physical — a body part — or behavioral — a thing the animal does? [pause] Then two detective questions!
All sorted, detective! [pause] Now show what you know.
Not quite. [pause] Ask: is it a body part the animal was born with, or an action it takes?
Not quite. [pause] Match the trick to the home. What would help an animal hide and stay alive in <emphasis>this</emphasis> place?
Not quite. [pause] A fossil is never just a rock — it is a clue. Ask: where does that animal live?
Yes! Stripes are a body pattern the tiger was born with — physical.
Yes! Hunting together is a thing wolves do — behavioral. No body part does it for them.
Yes! Fur grows on the body — a physical adaptation Rikki-tikki was born with.
Yes! Playing dead is an act the opossum performs — behavioral.
Yes! Claws are body parts — physical.
Yes! Flying south is a journey the geese make — behavioral.
Yes! White fur vanishes against snow — the right trick for this home. Adaptations fit the habitat.
Yes! A fossil is a clue: fish live in water, so this high ground was once a sea floor — long, long ago.
The tiger's stripes hide it in tall grass. What kind of adaptation?
Wolves hunt in a pack. What kind of adaptation?
One year, only big hard seeds are left. How does the bird population end up with bigger beaks?
High on a mountain you find a fish fossil. What does it tell you?
Why does Rikki-tikki the mongoose beat the cobra?
You can read an animal like a detective! [pause] Well done.
Good try! Let's watch the adaptations once more.
Lesson done! Now open research and look up the real mongoose. Find two adaptations the story got right, and save them in notebooks.
